content: Hearing loss in infants refers to the complete or partial inability to perceive sound in one or both ears. This condition can manifest in various ways depending on the infant's age and developmental stage. Symptoms of Hearing Loss in Infants A newborn with hearing loss may not startle or react to loud noises occurring nearby. Older infants, who are expected to respond to familiar voices, may show no reaction when spoken to. By 15 months of age, children should typically be using single words, and by age 2, they should be forming simple two-word sentences. Failure to meet these milestones may indicate hearing loss that has been present since infancy. Some children with hearing loss may not be diagnosed until they reach school age, even if the condition was present at birth. Undiagnosed hearing loss can lead to inattentiveness and academic difficulties. Causes of Hearing Loss in Infants Hearing loss can develop in children who initially had normal hearing. It may affect one or both ears and can range from mild to profound. Profound hearing loss is often referred to as deafness. Some cases of hearing loss are progressive, worsening over time, while others remain stable. There are four main types of hearing loss: 1. Conductive Hearing Loss (CHL): This occurs due to issues in the outer or middle ear, such as earwax buildup, eardrum rupture, or repeated infections. CHL is often treatable with medication or surgery. Causes in infants include: Structural abnormalities in the ear canal or middle ear Earwax buildup Repeated ear infections Foreign objects in the ear Ear injuries Eardrum rupture Tumors 2. Sensorineural Hearing Loss (SNHL): This results from problems in the inner ear, which is responsible for transmitting signals to the auditory nerve. SNHL is not curable, but hearing aids or cochlear implants may help. Causes include: Exposure to toxic chemicals or medications during pregnancy or after birth Genetic conditions, such as Down syndrome Infections before birth, such as cytomegalovirus or German measles during early pregnancy Post-birth infections, such as bacterial meningitis Structural abnormalities of the inner ear 3. Mixed Hearing Loss: This is a combination of conductive and sensorineural hearing loss, with causes stemming from a mix of the above factors. 4. Central Hearing Loss: This rare type results from damage to the auditory nerve or brain pathways that process sound. Causes include: Diseases affecting the myelin sheath (the protective coating around nerve cells) Tumors Risk Factors for Infant Hearing Loss A family history of hearing loss Infections caused by certain viruses or bacteria Low birth weight Structural abnormalities in the skull bones Approximately 2 to 3 infants out of every 1,000 live births are born with some degree of hearing loss. Diagnosis Hearing loss in infants is identified when a baby cannot hear sounds below a certain threshold. A healthcare provider will examine the child, looking for issues such as bone abnormalities or genetic changes that may contribute to hearing loss. An otoscope is used to inspect the baby’s ears, allowing the doctor to view the eardrum and identify potential causes of conductive hearing loss. Two common tests for newborn hearing screening include: 1. Auditory Brainstem Response (ABR) Test: This test uses electrodes to measure how the auditory nerve responds to sound. 2. Otoacoustic Emissions (OAE) Test: Microphones placed in the baby’s ears detect sound echoes in the ear canal. A lack of echo suggests hearing loss. For older infants and young children, tests such as visual response audiometry and play audiometry can assess their hearing range by teaching them to respond to sounds through play. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care Contact your healthcare provider if your baby or young child shows signs of hearing loss, such as not reacting to loud noises, not mimicking sounds, or not speaking at the expected age. If your child has a cochlear implant, seek immediate medical attention if they develop symptoms like fever, stiff neck, headache, or an ear infection. Treatment Options In the United States, over 30 states mandate newborn hearing screenings. Early treatment of hearing loss can enable many infants to develop normal language skills without delay. For infants born with hearing loss, treatment should ideally begin by 6 months of age. Treatment depends on the cause and severity of the hearing loss and may include: Speech therapy Learning sign language Cochlear implants for profound sensorineural hearing loss Addressing the underlying cause of hearing loss may involve: Medications for infections Ear tubes for recurrent ear infections Surgery to correct structural problems Prognosis The outcome for infants with hearing loss depends on the cause and severity of the condition. Advances in hearing aid technology and speech therapy allow many children to develop language skills on par with their peers. Even infants with profound hearing loss can achieve good outcomes with appropriate treatment. If the hearing loss is part of a broader disorder, the prognosis will depend on the specific condition and its effects on the body. Possible Complications Complications of hearing loss in infants include: Delayed speech and language development Difficulty forming friendships Emotional challenges due to feelings of isolation Academic struggles If hearing loss is associated with a syndrome or disease, additional complications specific to that condition may arise. Children with cochlear implants may have an increased risk of bacterial meningitis, an inflammation around the brain that can spread through the bloodstream. Vaccinations against bacteria that cause meningitis are available and may reduce this risk. Consult your healthcare provider for guidance. Prevention While not all cases of hearing loss in infants can be prevented, certain measures can reduce the risk: Women planning pregnancy should ensure they are up to date on vaccinations. Pregnant women should consult their doctor before taking any medications. Pregnant women should avoid activities that could expose their baby to dangerous infections, such as toxoplasmosis. Couples with a family history of hearing loss may consider genetic counseling before pregnancy.
